headline: The timing fault you picked is fixed. Our speed measurements could report an interrupt costing more than the whole frame that contained it — now each frame is charged what actually ran in it.
matters: Anyone reading our per-frame speed figures was at risk of chasing a spike that had been moved there from the frame before. The engine team had three measurement tools held back over this; they can now judge whether to move them. The fix also turned up that a feature they asked us to build would not have given them what they wanted, so I have flagged it rather than building it.
detail: Q-PROF-STRADDLE settled as a DEFECT (fork A), merged 51143a5 from branch prof-straddle. Root cause: the per-frame ring cut hintCycles/vintCycles from pending_buckets[level].cycles, an INCLUSIVE figure, and inclusive time only reaches a parent when the callee pops. Because the acknowledge arms a routine frame for the handler's own entry address, a bucket's ENTIRE cost is child time and none reaches the bucket before the RTE — so a straddling handler gave frame N the exception entry alone and frame N+1 the whole span. Fix charges the split on the self side via Frame::enclosing_bucket (stack index of innermost bucket, O(1) at push) + Profiler::pending_bucket_retired, accumulated only while the ring is armed. VERIFIED FIRSTHAND AT THIS SEAT, not accepted on report: full workspace suite 1809 passed / 0 failed / 6 ignored exit 0; red-first REPRODUCED by checking out 68461a7 into a scratch worktree and running it — 37 passed / 2 failed with failure output showing vint_cycles 40 against frame cycles 30, and 80 against 50, i.e. an interrupt costing more than its containing frame, which is what makes it arithmetic rather than taste; merged tree re-verified 41/0. Currency unmoved — golden_frames 7/0, scanline goldens, conformance_roms 3/0 in 41.7s of real work (checked for the silent-skip failure this repo has booked; vendor symlink present, no SKIP markers), schema_conformance 21/0 so no wire drift. RETRACTIONS the agent made against our own records, both correct: the mechanism doc's own SS2 'correction' was wrong (it reasoned from the generic parent/child rule and never asked what a bucket's children ARE), so the original SS3.3(a) finding was right; and SS3/SS6 rested on 'a bucket's cyclesSelf is lag-free', which is true and useless — corroborated by a PRE-EXISTING test, a_nested_hint_inside_a_vint_charges_the_inner_bucket_alone, pinning hint.self_cycles at one STEP_CYCLES against hint.cycles of three. That undercuts PROF-RING-SELF as specified; recommendation to refuse recorded, owner's call, not built. Also merged: new overseer bar that agents must not edit lane-status.json, after this one wrote an enum the suite contract does not define.

headline: Told aeon not to build the profiler field they asked for — and proved why on their own game rather than arguing it.
matters: They wanted a per-frame number showing what each interrupt cost. The field as they specified it would have been a constant: measured on their own ROM, it comes out to exactly 44 for both kinds of interrupt, even though one genuinely costs 19 times more than the other. It would have printed the same value during a slowdown as without one — a field that looks like the answer and is not. The number they actually want is one they already read, and it now accounts for every last cycle exactly. Building it would have cost real time and left them measuring nothing; the honest refusal is the more useful delivery.

Also the first on-machine validation of the straddle fix (4111c88 / merge 51143a5), which §7 of the mechanism doc settled on synthetic streams only. headline: We can't honestly say which game object a clicked sprite is — and now we know exactly why, and what would fix it.
matters: You wanted to click something in the game window and be told what it is. The emulator can see which hardware sprite you clicked, and it can read the game's object list, but nothing in the running machine connects the two — the engine draws the sprites and keeps no record of which object drew which. Every shortcut for guessing it fails on rings, which are the thing you are most likely to click and which are not objects at all, so a guess would confidently name the wrong thing with nothing to warn you. So the window will say plainly that it cannot tell you, rather than inventing an answer. The fix is small and it lives in the engine, not here: one debug-only list, 160 bytes, that writes down which object drew each sprite as it draws it. That ask is now with the engine lane, priced, with the line numbers checked against their tree. If they take it, clicking an object works properly and can even tell when the picture has moved on since you clicked.

headline: Tools can now write into video memory — through the path that keeps the sprite table honest, not the shortcut that would have lied.
matters: The editor and the engine lane both want to push artwork straight into the running machine to see it immediately, without a rebuild. There was already a shortcut in the code that looked like the obvious way to do it, and using it would have quietly broken things: the emulator keeps a small cached copy of where each sprite is, and the shortcut skips updating it, so the machine would have drawn a picture that its own memory did not describe. The new path keeps that copy in step. Three places where the written-down rules are silent - whether this should be refused while the game is running, what addresses it may touch, how much it may write at once - were implemented as the rules actually read and filed as questions upstream, rather than being quietly decided here. That order matters: adding a refusal later is easy, removing one people have built on is not.

headline: When the debugger stops the game, it sometimes stops a little late — and we found someone had already measured how often.
matters: Stopping the game at an exact instruction is the core of debugging, and until now nothing told you whether the stop landed where you asked or slightly past it. We proposed that every emulator must declare its own precision up front. While checking whether the problem was still real, an agent went looking in the old emulator's own documentation and found it had been measured years back and written down: most stops are exact, but one trial in four stopped 98 bytes early. That single fact changed the design from a preference into a requirement - if the imprecision comes and goes, you cannot learn about it by watching, because four good stops tell you nothing about the fifth. So a server has to promise its worst case rather than describe its usual one. The proposal is honest about its own weakness: everyone using this today is on the old emulator that is being retired, so it makes their move across checkable rather than making today better.

headline: Breakpoints work on the new emulator — you can stop the game on an exact instruction and look around.
matters: This is the thing a developer reaches for most and the new emulator did not have it at all. Five commands now work: set a stop point, turn it on or off, list what is armed, clear it, and wait for the game to hit one. It takes the list of missing commands from fifteen down to ten. The care went into one decision that would have been invisible if it had gone wrong: when a client asks to wait for the game to stop, the waiting happens on that client's own connection rather than inside the emulator, because the emulator is what has to keep running to REACH the stop point - a wait done the naive way would have frozen your player window for up to five minutes and then timed out having never moved. Testing also caught the emulator telling two different stories at once: it kept running while every reply said it had stopped, which showed up as 374,011 stops recorded where there should have been one. One honest limitation: a stop point does not fire while the player window is running the game freely on its own. It works everywhere else, including every tool that would use it, and I would rather tell you than let you find out.

headline: Breakpoints now work in your player window — before this, they could not fire at all while you were playing.
matters: Last night's breakpoint work shipped with a limitation I told you about: a stop point would not fire while your game window was running the game freely. I sent an agent to work out how the emulator should honestly SAY that, and the answer came back that there was nothing honest to say. The gap was not partial, it was total: while you were actually playing, a stop point could not fire by any route. Publishing that would have amounted to announcing that the debugger does not work while you debug. So I closed it instead. Your window now stops itself when a stop point is hit, the same way it does when you pause by hand, and it announces the stop to any tool watching. The note that had deferred this priced it as expensive; that was wrong, and the code's own comments said so while the note said otherwise - both pieces it claimed were missing already existed. I proved it works by driving the rebuilt program myself, but that test drove the emulator on its own rather than inside your window; the in-window behaviour is covered by an automated test rather than by me watching a real window, because the only two windows on this machine right now are yours and the editor's, and driving either would disturb your work. headline: I nearly raised a false alarm about our own program being out of date. The alarm was my measuring tool, not the program.
matters: The engine lane was about to rename part of how their tools talk to our emulator, and I checked our side was ready first. It was. But while checking I searched our built program for three pieces of text it should contain, and all three came back missing - which would have meant we were shipping something older than we thought, right as they were about to depend on it. I ran the search five different ways to be sure. All five agreed, and all five were wrong: when the compiler builds the fast version of a program it stores short pieces of text in a form a search cannot see. The engine lane settled it in one command by starting the program and asking it directly, which is the thing I had been avoiding. Two lessons, and the second is the uncomfortable one. First, searching a built program is not a substitute for running it - and it fails in the direction that invents problems. Second, a number I had measured days ago travelled to their notes, came back to me as if it were theirs, and I used it to argue against my own finding. Reading it carefully out of their files did not protect me, because careful reading confirms that a number was copied correctly, not that it was ever right.

headline: A peer found a hole in how we prove the emulator is honest about which build it is, and it was real.
matters: When a tool connects to the emulator, the emulator tells it which exact build of itself is answering - the commit it was built from, and whether that code had uncommitted edits. The editor lane spotted it by reading our tests against each other, which is a thing none of the tests' authors could have done from inside their own. headline: Your click-to-select-and-spawn idea: the hard half is proven working, and the engine lane's job just shrank to nothing for the first stage.
matters: You asked whether we could click things in the running game to select them and click places to spawn them. The engine lane's whole estimate hung on one question: does our click land on an actual game object, or only on a coloured pixel? If the engine had to answer that, their side was a big job. I proved it on a live game instead of guessing: clicking the player told us it was slot 0, 'Player_Main', with its position - and clicking the two rings on screen correctly answered 'that is not an object' rather than confidently naming the wrong one. Clicking a spot also gives its position in the level exactly, checked against where the game itself thinks the player is. All of that uses things the emulator already does, so for the first stage - click to select and inspect - the engine needs no changes at all, and the one thing I had asked them for turned out to be unnecessary and is withdrawn. Two traps found and written into the design so nobody walks into them later: two of the three sprites on screen were rings, so the guard against misreading them matters on the very first click, not in some rare case; and the game's camera lives at a different memory address in the debug build than the shipped one, which would silently place every click in the wrong spot for anyone who wrote the address down instead of looking it up. headline: Click-to-select is built: clicking a spot in the running game now tells you which object drew it, and where that is in the level.
matters: The first half of your click-to-select idea works. Ask the emulator about any dot on screen and it answers three things: which layer you are looking at, where that point sits in the level, and which object slot painted it. The care went into the five different ways the answer can be 'not an object', which sound like pedantry and are not: a ring is drawn differently from a normal object, and on the first real screen this was tried, two of the three things on screen were rings. If the emulator treated a ring like an object it would confidently name the WRONG object rather than admit it did not know - and you would have no way to tell. The same care covers your shipped game versus your debug build: on a shipped build it says 'this build cannot answer that' instead of 'there is nothing there'. Two checks that no automatic rule could catch shipped alongside it, because both are about the emulator telling the truth rather than about the shape of its answer. Also: it looks up where things live in memory every single time rather than remembering, because those addresses MOVE between your debug and shipped builds - and a remembered one gives a wrong answer that looks completely normal. I proved that one by deliberately breaking it: the broken version returned a perfectly plausible position, with no error at all. The spawn half - clicking to place things - is not built and still waits on the engine lane.

headline: The engine lane found a real bug in our emulator, and the right answer turned out to be NOT fixing it.
matters: They reported that clicking a pixel gives the right palette slot but the wrong colour, on any screen where the game changes colours partway down the picture. It is real - I reproduced it on a different test game by a different method, 55 out of 55 sample points wrong. Then I read the rulebook for that command and it says, in as many words, that this command must NOT read the drawn picture, and that this exact disagreement is deliberate and must not be papered over - it names the other command a person should use instead, which is the one the engine lane had already found for themselves. What was actually broken is smaller and real: the answer never tells you which moment its colour belongs to, so two fields quietly disagree and you cannot tell. That is a change to the agreed rules rather than to our code, and it is what I will write next. Two small things did land - a test that pins the behaviour AND explains why the tempting fix is wrong, so the next person does not repeat me, and a note about a rounding convention that was silently making correct pixels look wrong.

headline: The old emulator never checks what it is asked to do - misspell an address and it writes to address zero and says it worked.
matters: The debugging tools every lane in the suite uses still talk to that old server. There is no error for a mistyped parameter anywhere in it: six of its commands quietly fall back to address zero or value zero and reply success. This is the strongest argument yet for finishing the move to the new one, and it is the sentence your README should carry rather than the vaguer 'the surface is legacy' one. Nothing is known to have been bitten by it - this is the exposure, not an incident.
detail: F-LEGACY-SILENT-DEFAULT, docs/2026-08-30-legacy-silent-default.md. oracle-old/linux-port/gui/ControlSocket.cpp:130 getInt(k, d=0) returns d on absent key, unparseable string (catch(...)) and unhandled type; no unknown-key rejection in the file, verified as genuine absence under a positive control (grep -q exit 1, control exit 0). 34 call sites, 8 with no explicit default, 2 of those has()-guarded (:1954,:1959), leaving 6 unguarded and all on memory paths (:348,:702,:726,:782 addr; :615,:739 value). aeon's :894 timeout_ms/30000 confirmed. headline: Corrected my own finding from this morning: the old emulator ignores 63 parameters, not 34 - and a peer found that by accident.

I found out because the engine team swept the file more broadly for their own reasons, not because anyone checked my work. headline: Closed the count on the old emulator at 64 parameter reads, and found one route that does the OPPOSITE of what the caller asked.
matters: The count is now complete rather than climbing - we swept every way that server can reach a parameter, so nobody has to wonder if there is a 65th. The new one is the sharpest yet: ask it to enable a graphics layer while spelling the value in a way it does not recognise, and it mutes the layer instead, reporting success. It does echo back what it decided, so a careful caller can catch it. Also worth recording that I nearly published a second inversion that was not real - three spots looked unguarded and were guarded two lines up.
detail: Population closed at 64 = 63 accessor sites + ParseButtons :1576 (the only type-checking read; misspelled 'buttons' presses nothing, returns success). Type gap: has() :117 true for any present non-null; getBool :156 accepts only true/1/yes from a string, else d. So {'enabled':'on'} passes the explicit has-guard at :1523/:1567/:1925, reads false, *flag=!on mutes. Mitigated by addBool('enabled',on) echo. headline: Retracted this morning's finding and replaced it: I named the wrong four commands, and the reason I got it wrong is the same reason twice.

Send a nonsense address as text and every one of them quietly turns it into zero. The engine team found my error, and their own confirmation of it had been hollow - they checked the lines I cited existed rather than that they said what I claimed.

headline: Built the engine team their tool, and it immediately found two hazards that four rounds of careful hand-checking had missed.
matters: The whole point was to stop people hand-deriving this, and it proved itself on the first run. If a number arrives as text with junk on the end - '12abc' - the old server reads 12, which is neither what you meant nor the safe fallback anyone assumed. And if the parameter block itself is malformed, every value in the request silently becomes its default. Nobody had either, across a full day of two lanes checking each other. It also caught my own framing being too narrow: the danger is not confined to memory commands.

headline: Six fixes in your player window - including the dull sound, which now remembers your setting instead of asking you every time.

headline: The debugger now tells any tool that stops it how precise that stop was - and the claim is proven against the machine, not asserted.
matters: When a debugging tool halts the game to look at something, it could not previously tell whether the instruction that caused the halt had already run. That is the difference between reading a value before and after it changes, and getting it wrong silently is how a tool draws a confident wrong conclusion. Every halt now says which it is. The important part is HOW: rather than trusting our own code comments, the work arms real stops on a purpose-built test program, halts, and reads a register to see what actually happened. One of the seven kinds of halt turned out to be the later kind, and is now labelled honestly instead of optimistically. The morning's one failing check is also gone, and the whole suite is green.
detail: Merged 25621a9 (parcel/stopprecision, 7 commits) serving protocol 11.31, adopted by the hub from this lane's own CR-E filing at empyrean 82982b7. Seven reasons; entry is NOT emitted and correctly has no entry. MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: six exact, watchpoint afterCommit, on a purpose-built testrom fixture whose every instruction boundary is distinguishable. VERIFIED HERE FIRSTHAND, not on report: (1) the pinned blob 125d17f03ac33872d97dac9587f01a8e708b27da equals empyrean's own object at 82982b7, checked three ways; (2) the exact declaration does NOT rest on sampling - I read BreakStop in source (breakpoints.rs:211-238), it matches pc against the armed set at a boundary taken BEFORE the step with no cycle budget, deadline or approximation, which is the structural argument rule 3 demands since 8 trials cannot prove invariance; (3) prove_item24 classifies real register state and holds the server to the value the EVENT carried, not to the declaration; (4) the LIVE release server's handshake, read over a socket, returns the map top-level with breakpoint present and entry absent. Gates on the merged tree: fmt clean, clippy -D warnings clean, one cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast = 64 result lines, 2026 passed / 0 FAILED / 6 ignored, reconciled against the c771ade baseline (63/2013/1/6) as +1 suite line, +13 passed (8 stop_precision + 2 testrom + 3 schema_conformance 20->23), -1 failed. AGENT'S OWN BEST FINDING: its test raced (resume reply vs the stopped event, which Client::ok discards) and failed at trial 4 of 8 AFTER three clean passes - a single-shot test would have been green forever; registered F-RESUME-STOP-RACE, still live in breakpoints.rs/watchpoints.rs. headline: The window now says when something can stop the game, that it just did, and how to start it again — and the line that was supposed to tell you that had been naming the wrong things.
matters: The night it looked stuck, there WAS a line on the top bar claiming to say what was armed to stop the machine. It counted watchpoints and the profiler — neither of which can freeze that window — and never mentioned breakpoints, which are the only thing that can. So the one place you could have looked was pointing away from the cause. It is renamed, a test now forbids that line from saying stop, halt or armed, and a real alarm with a release button sits on the top bar where it is visible no matter which tab you are on. Three things I told the agent were wrong and it measured them rather than believing me: the halt re-fires on every resume, not every frame, which is why the surface counts halts instead of flashing once; and there is a second place a halt can happen that I did not know about, where a tool drives a bounded run — recording only the first would have made the window confidently report a fresh halt as thousands of frames old.

headline: A debugger tool could tell you the machine never stopped, after waiting no time at all — and only in the window you actually play in.
matters: Anyone waiting on a breakpoint could be told 'it never happened' a fraction of a second after asking, with the game still running. It looked like a flaky test for two nights and was written off as one twice. It was never flaky: it failed only on the wait that follows a resume, which is what named the cause.
detail: Merge d5a66ae on main, pushed (6a73776 -> d5a66ae, remote confirmed moved by fetch; d5a66ae is an ancestor of origin/main). Branch parcel/waitforbreak-instant-timeout, 2 commits (fc9bb5b fix+tests, 90b08e5 doc-only measurement), +609/-58 across oracle-aether src/server.rs, src/host.rs, src/engine.rs, tests/hosted.rs. ROOT CAUSE: Host::pump published SharedStamp at the END of the drain, after reply.send, so a client holding the resume reply could send wait_for_break while the stamp still carried running:false from the prior halt; the connection thread's poll exited at ~0ms and the engine, re-reading the live flag, answered timeoutReached:true. server::engine_loop always published before its reply; Host::pump, the second run driver, did not - so the standalone server never had this and only the hosted path did. THE FALSE COMMENT WAS THE BUG: engine.rs asserted the two halves 'agree by construction'; they read ONE quantity (Engine::is_running/free_run) down TWO channels, live flag vs published snapshot, and a snapshot can be stale in the wrong direction. Corrected in place plus two adjacent stale claims (SharedStamp's 'only ever used for errors the engine never saw' - the wait is its second reader; and 'at most one frame stale ... costs one frame of latency and nothing else' - true only of a stale-true). FIX is two layers, both kept: Host::publish_stamp called before every reply (matches engine_loop), and server::dispatch_call treats timeoutReached:true arriving before the budget is spent as evidence of a stale stamp rather than an answer, re-syncing and resuming the wait, bounded by the caller's own budget. Ablation says layer 2 alone closes it; layer 1 kept so the method does not rest on an ordering invariant in another file, which is the mistake the old comment made. Reproduction 7/30 whole-suite runs under load pre-fix, 0/30 post-fix, 0/30 unloaded, ~300 spinners load avg ~250; all 7 failed at the SECOND wait (post-resume), never the first (post-halt). Wire capture pre-fix: {'running':true,'timeoutReached':true,'waitedMs':0} against timeoutMs 10000. Three red-first mutations each quoted from disk and restored from committed baseline fc9bb5b. All six preservation constraints tested: engine thread never blocks, two clients wait at once, pump never frozen, timeoutMs:0 polls once, paused machine answers at once and is never resumed, over-ceiling refused -32602 and never retried. waitedMs emission unchanged on the error path (verified against main: both old and new insert only on Ok(Object)). MY GATE on the merged tree: fmt clean, clippy x2 zero, LEGS=66 PASSED=2253 FAILED=0 IGNORED=6, exit 0, HEAD_AT_START==HEAD_AT_END==d5a66ae; baseline was 66/2245 so +8 is exactly the 7 server::wait_tests rows plus 1 host::tests row, and all six named tests confirmed present in my own run log rather than inferred from the total. Brief corrections the agent made against me, both accepted: the provenance was TWO sightings not one (lane-log line 73, 2026-09-03T03:35:56Z, already tagged it a load-sensitive flake), and neither log entry recorded the failing assertion, so 'instant timeout' was an inference off source presented in the brief as evidence. My two-different-flags hypothesis was wrong; the premise of the code comment was true and its conclusion was false.

headline: Two things booked as bugs in our emulator turned out never to have been ours, and the note that said otherwise is fixed.
matters: A fortnight ago we wrote down two faults in how the sound-chip memory window handles an oversized request - a write running off the end silently wrapping to the start, and a too-large read quietly returning less than asked without saying so. Both were real, but in the OLD emulator we are replacing, not in ours: ours was built later specifically to refuse them, and does. I confirmed that on the running program rather than from the code, including a control to prove the check could actually have seen a fault. The note never said which of the two emulators it meant, so it read as ours, and today it sent me chasing them. That wording problem is the durable finding and I have fixed it in both places it appeared.
detail: Foreground runtime pass, taken the moment a lane-owned emulator instance existed (the MCP shim was alive this session as own-instance with romFreshness verified, contradicting the banked claim that a /clear cannot restore it - measurement wins, flagged to the hub). CONTROL RUN per bar 16(d): a 4-byte write at $3FFC did land at $1FFC and the read channel saw it, so the unchanged reading is a measurement not a blind probe; restored to baseline after. headline: The step command now tells you how many instructions really ran, and refuses the counts it had been wrongly accepting for ten days.
matters: Asking the debugger to step further than it can manage in one go used to give you an answer that looked like success, with no way to tell it had stopped early - so you could read a number of instructions as having run when they had not. It now reports the real figure. Separately, it had been accepting a step of zero and a step of a million-and-one, both of which the written contract says must be refused; a comment beside the code claimed it followed that contract exactly. It does now.
detail: CR-STEP-SHORTFALL, all three halves. Merge fae868f on main, parcel tip b7043a0 (9f49e31 code+tests+re-vendor, 470c454 board, b7043a0 ledger). Serves protocol.md 11.33's `stepped` (integer >=1, the instructions actually retired) on emulator/step only - set at exactly one site inside fn step, NOT in the shared halt_result, so step_over/step_out are untouched per 11.33's explicit non-amendment, with a test asserting their absence that carries its own control so it cannot pass by the key being dropped everywhere. The retire tally increments from the core's own on_step_retire callback BEFORE the fired guard, never from count - the agent rejected plumbing count-minus-remaining as 'the handler's arithmetic wearing a witness's clothes', which is this lane's parity-pair bar applied unprompted. count bounds 0..u64::MAX -> 1..=1_000_000. Re-vendored bus-protocol.schema.json at empyrean 8a930919 (blob 41ec6470, 347476 B, sha256 and git-hash-object both re-verified here against the written file); PROVENANCE.md's machine pin AND its stale human table both corrected - the table had still described the previous re-vendor (e04a94f/487af407/345965 B) while the gate read the correct pin, so it was green and the prose lied. AGENT CORRECTED ME ON FOUR POINTS, all accepted: (1) 3b43185e does NOT carry the schema - it touches protocol.md and vectors.json only - so pin.revision is 8a930919, the commit that actually wrote the bytes; my brief was wrong and would have pinned a commit that never wrote them. (2) FOUR tests carried the superseded reading, not the two I named; the third was invisible to a grep for the rot's own words because it USED count:0 as a look-without-moving device while its text said nothing about bounds. (3) advance_stepping did not already know the retired count. (4) `stepped` minimum:1 cannot express a step that retired nothing (a CPU halted on STOP) - key omitted there, documented in three places, OWED UPSTREAM as a minimum:0 amendment. Ledger L-04 and L-03 item 4 close; L-04 records that our own banked position on the count floor was ruled against, and it is the position that cost the ten days. Error-surface gate's claim to this defect as its demonstration was SOFTENED by the agent rather than banked. headline: Asked to step a machine that is halted, the debugger used to claim it ran a million instructions. It now says it ran none.
matters: This was found only because we went to serve an honest zero. Yesterday's work added a line saying how many instructions really ran, and left one case unspellable: a processor stopped dead, waiting, executes nothing, and the rules had no way to write that down. The contract team fixed the rules within the hour. Taking that up, the agent measured the case before changing anything - and the answer was not silence, it was a lie: ask it to step a million instructions on a halted machine and it reported a million, with the machine visibly not having moved. A stopped processor still gets asked 'anything yet?' every cycle, and we were counting each of those as an instruction. Two related commands had the same fault from the other direction - they reported success instantly for a call that never happened.
detail: STEPPED-FLOOR-ZERO. Merge 0d11908 on main, parcel tip ac43e14. Re-vendored bus-protocol.schema.json at empyrean bbf3bf8 (blob d383daeb, 347676 B) taking stepped's floor 1 -> 0; pin block AND human table re-derived by parsing the written copy. THE REAL FIX, beyond the parcel I briefed: measured pre-change, step{count:1000000} on a CPU halted at stop #$2700 returned stepped:1000000 with pc unmoved at 0x288 - wrong output, not an omission, so deleting the guard alone would have left it and I would have banked 'the halted case now gets its honest 0' while it returned count. Root cause: a Stopped CPU still turns the crank and the core emits a retire per idle slice. New StepRetire::idle / StepOutcome::idle_slice in oracle-core, set at exactly the two CpuState arms that produce an idle slice; StepStop::on_step_retire excludes them from tally AND goal. `executed` was the wrong flag to reuse - it is false for three unlike things (exception entry, aborted instruction, idle slice) and only the third must not count. Excluding from the goal too is deliberate: otherwise a halted step{count:1} 'meets its condition' on a turn where nothing happened and reports deadlineReached:false while the reply says stepped:0 - reply and event contradicting. RULED BY ME, no follow-up work: the resulting latency (a step on a halted CPU now spends its frame budget, ~3s, and this reaches step_over/step_out which previously returned instantly) is correct rather than merely conservative - a STOPped CPU can be woken by an interrupt during those frames and then instructions genuinely retire, and there is no cheap safe short-circuit since even a fully-masked STOP is wakeable by a level-7 NMI. step_over/step_out returning at once on the first idle was itself a wrong answer (success for a call that never completed). MY GATE on the merged tree: fmt 0, clippy x2 zero both runs, LEGS=66 PASSED=2285 FAILED=0 IGNORED=6, TEST_EXIT=0, HEAD_AT_START==HEAD_AT_END==0d11908. Baseline 2284, +1 = the one new row, confirmed by name in my own log with both controls behaving; the second added fn (halted_mclk) confirmed a helper by reading it, 21 #[test] vs 28 top-level fns. Agent corrected me on six points incl. that the ADOPTED CONTRACT TEXT's justification ('a CPU already halted on STOP retires nothing') is true of hardware and was false of this server - nobody in the chain had run the case - and that two schema leaves moved, not the one upstream's additivity paragraph names (description grew 1012->1212 chars; no validation force, so flagged not escalated). The two crates/oracle-core/tests/ movers are new-field initialisers, a compile requirement not a currency change, recorded as a named decision in the merge message.

headline: Clicking outside the level now tells you so, instead of accepting the click and quietly binning the object.

The window now checks before it sends, and says which of three things happened: your click was outside the level (and it tells you how big the level is), or it cannot read the level's size so it will not guess, or no level is loaded yet. That last one exists because the level size reads as zero before a level starts, and telling somebody on a title screen that their click is 'outside the level' would send them looking for an edge that does not exist.

headline: Reloading a rebuilt game now warns you that the debugger is still using the old list of names, instead of silently doing it.
matters: This one bit me personally today and nearly made me report a fault against another team. They published two new names; I reloaded the game; the reload said it had succeeded and had NOT thrown away the name list - and then the debugger insisted the new names did not exist, while I was looking at them in the file. headline: The debugger can now tell you at any moment that its list of names may be out of date - and it is cheap enough to ask sixty times a second.
matters: This morning's fix only warned you at the moment you reloaded the game. The case that actually catches people is the other one: you connect once, leave it running, and the game gets rebuilt underneath you over the next few hours - you never reload, so you were never warned. The plain answer would have cost 15% of a processor core to keep asking, because checking means re-reading a 357 KB file. It now checks the file's identity first, which is about eleven thousand times cheaper, and only re-reads when something really moved.
detail: CR-K serve, closing the CR we filed and the contract team adopted the same day as 11.34. Merge 84bdf94 on main, parcel tip 7409820. Re-vendored at empyrean b447555 (blob 3f758c40, 348406 B), pin revision DERIVED via git log -1 -- the schema path and merge-base --is-ancestor RUN; parsing both blobs shows exactly one fragment changed (emulator/status gains caveat), 67 fragments and 19 $defs unmoved. Serve reuses the existing stale_symbols_caveat - one implementation, two consumers, and reload_rom was re-pointed at the same door so the two cannot answer one client differently about one file in one millisecond. THE PARCEL WAS THE COST, measured firsthand by the agent on the real listing (356,976 B / 6,690 lines / 2,970 rows, release, 200-sample mean): full check 2.566 ms, of which SymbolTable::parse is 2.558 ms; fs::metadata 222 ns. At 60 Hz the naive form is 154 ms/s = 15.4% of a core to answer the cheapest method on the bus; the fingerprint filter costs 13.3 us/s, ~11,500x cheaper. Fingerprint is (dev, ino, len, mtime, ctime) + path + symbols_generation, NOT size+mtime as I suggested: ctime is the field with teeth, since utimes() lets a caller choose mtime but always sets ctime, so cp -p / tar -x / rsync -t restoring an OLDER listing stays visible. Stated at the point of use is what it cannot see (a same-length rewrite inside one timestamp tick on a coarse filesystem; a clock moved backwards). Loud-on-unmeasurable is the default not a branch: nothing is cached unless the fingerprint was obtained. ORDERING, the agent's real-bug-risk flag: the fingerprint is taken BEFORE the read - taken after, a rewrite landing between read and stat would be recorded as describing bytes it does not describe and every later call would short-circuit onto a permanently stale quiet; before, the same race costs one wasted parse. headline: The test that only failed when the machine was busy turned out to be a real fault of ours, not noise - the third time this one was looked at and the first time it was believed.
matters: It had been written off as a flake twice. A test suite that fails only under load teaches people to re-run it until it passes, which is how a real fault hides in plain sight.
detail: F-HANDSHAKE-LOAD-TIMEOUT, merge 2f97626, tip 55d8326. NOT A FLAKE: reproduced 8/8 at load average 43-65 under 64 bounded spinners, 15/15 unloaded. Root cause: emulator/step_out has no frame to return out of on the sweep fixture, so it runs the engine's whole 600-frame step budget - 6.68s of a 7.44s sweep - inside ONE socket read whose deadline is 20s. The passing case had a 3x margin and nothing else; scheduler contention ate it. Confirmed on the wire by the server's own late stopped event (frame 600, deadlineReached true), so the server was starved, never hung. Fix: 1-frame budget for the sweeps plus re-pausing any row that leaves the machine running - booked test 7.58s -> 0.23s, margin 2.6x -> 87x, and 8/8 pass at load 68-72, HIGHER than the band that failed. The read timeout now names the outstanding method and distinguishes answered-LATE from never-answered, which is what made the cause visible and why this was misread twice. My free-run hypothesis was confirmed but MINOR - 0.56s, 7% of the cost, not the 90% I implied. THE BEST FINDING IS THE AGENT'S SELF-CATCH: it refactored the frame ceiling to derive from the budget constant because it read better, which made raising the budget also raise the ceiling - so the proven mutation came back GREEN IN 6.62 SECONDS, a dead check still paying the full runtime of the defect it no longer detected. Caught only by re-running the mutation AFTER the refactor. Red-first proves a check worked at that moment, not that it still works. It also caught its own new error message asserting 'hang or deadlock rather than slowness' - false at load 47, where a starved server missed both windows - and rewrote it to state what it ruled out. headline: A search tool we all rely on quietly hides results, and I worked out exactly when it hides all of them and when it hides only some.
matters: This is how several of us check that something is absent, which is how we decide a job is done or a risk is gone. It can report nothing found when there is something to find, and it never says so. Now pinned down well enough to know which situations are dangerous and how to check.
detail: Another lane found that grep on this machine is a harness shell function, not /usr/bin/grep, and skips gitignored files. It was described as returning a clean empty result. I measured it and got 6 hits against 13 for the identical pattern and path, so I corrected the shape to 'under-reports rather than empties' and the hub adopted that wording. THAT CORRECTION WAS ALSO WRONG, refuted by a data point inside the hub's own message (aeon's case reproducing at 0 against 343), and I retracted it: I had generalised a shape from n=1. Then tested the discriminator with a control in both directions, on a pattern present in exactly one gitignored file: from the repo root the shell grep returns 0 while /usr/bin/grep returns 1, a TOTAL false negative; naming target/ explicitly returns 1 and 1. So walking PAST an ignored directory prunes the subtree entirely, while naming it directly walks in and only the per-file filters bite, giving a partial miss of unpredictable size. One behaviour, two directions. The dangerous case is the ordinary one: searching the repo from its root for something that lives in build output returns a confident zero. RULE, stated so it does not depend on my mechanism being right: a recursive grep is unusable as a count or an absence over any possibly-ignored path until /usr/bin/grep on the identical path agrees. I re-verified my own two load-bearing absences under this, each with a positive control that fired: nothing depends on oracle-player (confirmed independently from the lockfile's dependency graph, which is what justified accepting a scoped gate), and the window surfaced no build identity before the parcel (0 hits while the same pattern found 5 in the server at the same revision). Both were taken with git grep over tracked source, which this hazard does not touch.
